title: Integrate security into the SDLC: decision comparison 1
teachingQuestion: How does a secure SDLC turn security from an end-stage review into evidence and feedback at every lifecycle stage, including retirement?
focalInsight: Security requirements, threat model, secure design, secure implementation/testing, deployment provenance, operations, retirement, and feedback.
caption: Compare meaning, decision conditions, and failures. These concise distinctions are paired with the worked examples in the teaching unit.

nodes.label: Sdlc
nodes.definition: The software development life cycle: coordinated phases from initiation and requirements through design, build, test, deployment, operation, and retirement.
nodes.decision: Put security decisions and evidence in each applicable phase and feed operational results into subsequent work.
nodes.failureExample: A project that ends controls at deployment leaves patching, monitoring, revocation, and disposal unmanaged.
nodes.detail: The software development life cycle: coordinated phases from initiation and requirements through design, build, test, deployment, operation, and retirement.

nodes.label: Security Requirements
nodes.definition: Testable security outcomes that constrain the product before design and implementation.
nodes.decision: Define requirements from asset value, threat, compliance, privacy, resilience, and owner needs, then trace them to evidence.
nodes.failureExample: A vague “secure API” requirement gives testers no criterion for access or audit behavior.
nodes.detail: Testable security outcomes that constrain the product before design and implementation.

nodes.label: Threat Modeling
nodes.definition: Attacker-oriented analysis of system boundaries, assets, entry points, abuse cases, and control assumptions.
nodes.decision: Use it at design and revisit it after material changes or operational evidence changes assumptions.
nodes.failureExample: An added partner integration can create replay/spoofing paths that the original model never assessed.
nodes.detail: Attacker-oriented analysis of system boundaries, assets, entry points, abuse cases, and control assumptions.

nodes.label: Waterfall
nodes.definition: A phased SDLC with formal baselines and milestone approvals before proceeding.
nodes.decision: Integrate security at initiation, requirements, design, test, and release gates; manage authorized rework when requirements change.
nodes.failureExample: A final-only security review may uncover an architectural flaw after the baseline is costly to change.
nodes.detail: A phased SDLC with formal baselines and milestone approvals before proceeding.

nodes.label: Agile
nodes.definition: Iterative lifecycle delivery in small, collaborative increments that can incorporate frequent feedback.
nodes.decision: Include security stories, acceptance criteria, threat-model updates, and tests in each increment.
nodes.failureExample: Deferring security stories to a final sprint recreates a late hardening phase.
nodes.detail: Iterative lifecycle delivery in small, collaborative increments that can incorporate frequent feedback.

nodes.label: Devops
nodes.definition: An approach that connects development and operations for rapid, reliable delivery and feedback.
nodes.decision: Use operational telemetry and ownership to inform delivery decisions, while keeping security evidence and release accountability.
nodes.failureExample: Fast automation without monitored rollback can spread a faulty configuration rapidly.
nodes.detail: An approach that connects development and operations for rapid, reliable delivery and feedback.

nodes.label: Devsecops
nodes.definition: Integration of security practices, people, and suitable automation into development and operations workflows.
nodes.decision: Use early automated checks where reliable, with accountable human review for risk, architecture, exceptions, and incident learning.
nodes.failureExample: A pipeline can pass static checks while the deployed authorization configuration is wrong.
nodes.detail: Integration of security practices, people, and suitable automation into development and operations workflows.

nodes.label: Shift Left
nodes.definition: Moving security analysis, requirements, design review, and defect discovery earlier in the lifecycle where change is cheaper and more influential.
nodes.decision: Apply it to discover issues before implementation while retaining runtime monitoring and feedback; it does not mean “only early security.”
nodes.failureExample: Treating shift-left as a substitute for production monitoring misses deployed configuration and abuse behavior.
nodes.detail: Moving security analysis, requirements, design review, and defect discovery earlier in the lifecycle where change is cheaper and more influential.

learningContract.misconception: Security is a testing phase after coding, or deployment ends security responsibility.
learningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.

learningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not mandate a specific framework, programming language, automated tool, or retention period.
learningContract.retrievalPrompt: A released partner API shows token replay attempts. Which lifecycle artifacts must change before the next release?
